sections.skill: Explain diversification and asset allocation and compute a portfolio's weighted return

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which portfolio is MOST diversified?

choices.text: Shares of one technology company
Three stocks, all airlines
A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
Shares of a single restaurant chain and its supplier

questions.correct_answer: A total market index fund plus a bond index fund
questions.intro: Diversification means spreading money across many investments so that a problem with one has a smaller effect on the whole. It can be across companies, industries, countries, and types of assets (stocks, bonds, cash). Diversification lowers risk but cannot eliminate it or guarantee against loss.
questions.feedback: Thousands of stocks plus bonds spread risk widely.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jen's portfolio is 60% stocks and 40% bonds. Stocks return 8% and bonds 3% this year. What is the portfolio's return?
questions.intro: Asset allocation is how a portfolio is divided among asset classes such as stocks, bonds, and cash. A portfolio's return is the weighted average: (weight × return) for each part, added together.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which statement about diversification is TRUE?

choices.text: A diversified portfolio cannot lose value
It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses
Diversification guarantees a profit every year
Owning more shares of one stock is diversification

questions.correct_answer: It reduces the impact of any single investment but cannot prevent all losses
questions.feedback: Broad market declines can still lower a diversified portfolio.

misconceptions.A: Assumes a diversified investment cannot lose value

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jen has $10,000 invested: 60% stocks, 40% bonds. How much is in stocks?
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Generally, which allocation fits a 20-year-old saving for retirement better than a 70-year-old retiree?

choices.text: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
All cash, because young people cannot handle risk
All bonds, because stocks are illegal for young investors
Exactly the same allocation for everyone

questions.correct_answer: More stocks, because the time horizon is longer
questions.intro: A longer time horizon allows more time to recover from stock market declines, so younger investors often hold more stocks. People nearing their goal often shift toward bonds and cash.
questions.feedback: Longer horizons can usually tolerate more stock market risk.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.relationship: Diversification is "don't put all your eggs in one basket"; students need the idea before the math.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A fruit stand sells only bananas. During a banana shortage it cannot get any bananas, so it cannot make sales. What happens?

choices.text: It is unaffected
It earns more because bananas are now scarce
Its insurance replaces the lost sales
Its whole business suffers

questions.intro: When all your money depends on one thing, a problem with that thing affects everything. Spreading out reduces the damage.
questions.feedback: With only one product and none to sell, the whole business is hit.

misconceptions.B: Ignores that it has no bananas to sell

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A second stand sells bananas, apples, and oranges. During a banana shortage it cannot get bananas, but it can still get and sell apples and oranges. What happens?

choices.text: Only part of its business suffers
Its whole business suffers just as much
It earns nothing at all
It earns more on every fruit

questions.correct_answer: Only part of its business suffers
questions.intro: Spreading sales across several products means a problem with one product affects only part of the business.
questions.feedback: Selling several fruits spreads the risk.

misconceptions.D: Assumes the shortage helps all products

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which saying describes diversification?

choices.text: "Buy low, sell high."
"Slow and steady wins the race."
"A penny saved is a penny earned, my friend."
"Don't put all your eggs in one basket."

questions.correct_answer: "Don't put all your eggs in one basket."
questions.feedback: Spreading eggs across baskets limits the damage if one falls.

misconceptions.A: A timing saying, not about spreading risk

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jen owns stocks of 20 U.S. companies and adds a bond fund. What kind of diversification does the bond fund add?

choices.text: Across brokerage firms
Across asset classes
Across account types
Across more companies only

questions.intro: Diversification can happen across companies, industries, countries, and asset classes (broad types of investments, such as stocks, bonds, and cash).
questions.feedback: Stocks and bonds are different asset classes.

misconceptions.A: Confuses where you invest with what you own
misconceptions.D: Bonds are a different asset class, not just more companies

sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: What is 40% of $5,000?
questions.intro: Percent of an amount = amount × rate as a decimal.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

sections.skill: Find a percent of a quantity
sections.relationship: Allocations are percents of a portfolio.

ref_skill.name: Find a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100

sections.skill: Find the mean of a data set
sections.relationship: A portfolio return is a weighted mean of its parts' returns.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jen's target is 60% stocks, 40% bonds on $10,000. After a strong year, she has $7,200 in stocks and $3,800 in bonds. What percent is in stocks now (nearest whole percent)?
questions.intro: Over time, investments grow at different rates, so a portfolio drifts away from its target allocation. Rebalancing means buying or selling to return to the target.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: To rebalance $11,000 to 60% stocks, what should the stock amount be?
questions.intro: Target amount = total value × target percent.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Jen's portfolio holds $7,200 in stocks, and her target for stocks is $6,600. How much stock should she sell (moving it to bonds)?
questions.intro: Amount to move = current amount − target amount.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Why rebalance?

choices.text: To guarantee higher returns
Because federal law requires it to be done each month
To keep risk at the level the investor chose
To avoid ever owning bonds

questions.correct_answer: To keep risk at the level the investor chose
questions.intro: Without rebalancing, a portfolio can become riskier than intended as stocks grow.
questions.feedback: Rebalancing restores the chosen risk level.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Instead of selling, Jen could rebalance by directing new contributions to bonds. Why might that be helpful in a taxable account?

choices.text: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
It earns guaranteed returns
It is required by the IRS
It removes all risk

questions.correct_answer: It can avoid selling and creating taxable gains
questions.intro: Selling investments at a gain in a taxable account can create capital gains taxes.
questions.feedback: Using new money to rebalance can avoid realizing gains.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Two stocks always rise and fall together. Does owning both diversify much?

choices.text: Yes, because there are now two different funds
Yes, completely
No, it doubles the risk
Not much, because they move the same way

questions.correct_answer: Not much, because they move the same way
questions.intro: Diversification works best when investments do not all move together. Assets that move the same way give little protection; assets that move differently reduce overall swings.
questions.feedback: Investments that move together provide little diversification.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Which pair is more likely to diversify a stock-heavy portfolio?

choices.text: Two technology stocks
Two airline stocks
Stocks and high-quality bonds
Two stock funds holding the same companies

questions.intro: High-quality bonds often behave differently from stocks, especially in downturns, though not always.
questions.feedback: High-quality bonds often move differently from stocks.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: Sam owns three different S&P 500 index funds. Is he well diversified across funds?

choices.text: Yes, owning three funds triples her overall diversification
Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
Yes, because each has a different name
No, because index funds hold one stock

questions.correct_answer: Not really; the three funds hold almost the same stocks
questions.intro: Funds that track the same index hold the same companies, so owning several adds little diversification.
questions.feedback: Overlapping funds add little real diversification.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: In a severe market crash, many stocks fall together. What does this show about diversification across stocks?

choices.text: Diversification always prevents losses
Diversified portfolios are immune to crashes
Bonds always fall more than stocks
It cannot remove market-wide risk

questions.intro: Market risk affects nearly all stocks at once; diversification mainly reduces the risk of individual companies or industries.
questions.feedback: Market-wide declines affect even diversified stock portfolios.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.

questions.domain: Investing, Brokerage Accounts, and Investment Products
questions.prompt: A target-date fund automatically shifts from stocks toward bonds as the target year approaches. What problem does it solve?

choices.text: It guarantees no losses before the target year
It removes all fees
It manages allocation and rebalancing for you
It invests only in cash

questions.correct_answer: It manages allocation and rebalancing for you
questions.intro: Target-date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds and become more conservative over time.
questions.feedback: Target-date funds automate allocation changes over time.
sources: Hypothetical example; no changing rule is used.
